title: Lacking a Code Makes You a Threat
author: Brandon Moore
summary: Brandon Moore writes to fathers about the necessity of having a personal code of ethics -- not for one's own sake, but because the absence of one makes a man a threat to those around him. Without guiding principles, natural strengths become corrupted: 'Strength becomes cruelty. Charisma twists into manipulation. Leadership becomes domination.' Moore shares his journey of recognizing that his lack of self-governance was frightening his family despite never being physically aggressive. His 'battle tested plan': when giving sons advice, honestly assess whether you embody the standard -- and then admit your failures to your son directly. Sons want to surpass their fathers in what they find admirable; giving them a genuinely held standard creates a legacy that compounds across generations.
points: * A man without a code is a threat to those around him -- his natural capacities become corrupting forces: 'Strength becomes cruelty. Charisma twists into manipulation. Leadership becomes domination.' * Moore: 'I had to learn that a man who answers to nothing, would do anything' -- the absence of ethical anchoring produces self-destructive behavior and harm to others. * Moore describes recognizing that his family was afraid of him despite no physical violence -- unpredictability and anger alone communicate threat when no code governs them. * Battle-tested plan for fathers: when giving sons advice, stop and ask whether you are an example -- if not, admit your failures honestly to your son, not defensively. * Sons want to outperform their fathers in what they find admirable; showing them the standard and daring them to exceed it creates cross-generational wealth of character. * A man's code is not about controlling his family but about 'a living form of discipline so that he can dare to be better than you.'
quotes: 'Strength' becomes cruelty. 'Charisma' twists into manipulation. 'Leadership' becomes domination.
I had to learn that a man who answers to nothing, would do anything.
One day I noticed my family was afraid of me. I had never hit them when angry, nor would I... but how did they know that?
Show him your rules aren't about control over him, but a living form of discipline so that he can dare to be better than you.
Never forget that sons want to outperform their fathers in every way they find admirable. Find out what he thinks is admirable about you. Then show him how to be even better than you.
This is how the metaphorical torch can be carried on for generations. It compounds into a sort of wealth.
